method: Convergence matrix, then narrative synthesis. Quantitative pooling was not offered because no finding estimates the same quantity on the same scale.

legend.D: dissonant (points the other way or changes with a definition)

conclusions.text: H1 cannot be tested as worded. No quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation. Q1 compares it with chat bots, Q3 refers only to having to "repeat yourself", and Q2 gives one indirect voice comparison: "sometimes when you are talking to a more of a robot, it sounds more like a robot voice".
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: Nine of ten techniques agree and TC1-16 agrees in part, because it finds Q2 an indirect voice comparison. The CK-17 spans that failed were labels, not source quotes, and a human review sample and a second coder were not done, which does not cap the label at this stakes.

conclusions.text: Reactions to the AI are split among the six quoted participants. P1 (Q1), P2 (Q2) and P3 (Q3) speak well of it, and P4 (Q5) moves from wanting to speak to someone to calling it a good process. P10 (Q4, Q8), P1 (Q6) and P5 (Q7) are unfavourable. The tally runs from a tie to four against two, depending on how P1 and P4 are coded and whether context-specific complaints count.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques report a split, and the sensitivity rows in TC1-17 change the size of the lean but never reverse it; no second coder or human review sample was used, which is named here and does not cap the label.

conclusions.text: The reasons participants give for negative reactions are specific features, not one cause. These are the voice and accent (Q4, Q7), the length of the introduction (Q8), a stressful setting (Q7) and earlier experience with AI agents (Q6). The material does not isolate learning that it is an AI as the cause, but P5 does name "AI in its current state" in Q7, and the link from Q7 to the motor claim scenario is inferred, not recorded.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Most techniques name the same drivers, but TC1-16 finds that Q4 and Q6 do not fit a single context explanation and that the scenario link is an inference; these are stated reasons, not tested causes.

conclusions.text: H2 is neither supported nor refuted. P10 says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro." (Q8) and gives the length of the introduction as the reason. P5 would probably have hung up only after not getting a human (Q10). No quote says a participant would stay on the line, and the one weak sign, P4 in Q5, is about a process and not about hanging up.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: The techniques split between contradicted for two participants and untested, and TC1-17 shows the verdict depends on whether hypothetical statements and the cause (learning it is an AI) are required; human review was not done and does not cap the label.

conclusions.text: H3 is not supported, and two participants say they would ask for a human. P5 says "I would've asked for a human." (Q10) with no timing. P4 says "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it" (Q9), which is hedged, and Q5 says the wish fades as the process goes on. No quote says a participant would decline to ask. Under a strict reading of "immediately" the contradiction falls to one participant or to none.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree on the loose reading, but TC1-16 and TC1-17 show it rests on two participants, on hypothetical and hedged statements, and on timing the quotes do not give; human review was not done and does not cap the label.

conclusions.text: The evidence is limited in ways every finding records. P8 and P9 have no quote, the basis for choosing the ten quotes is not given, every hang-up or human-request statement is a hypothetical reaction to a prerecorded scenario, and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed. Counts describe the selected quotes and not how common a view is.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques state these limits and they are stated in the material itself; the CK-17 spans that failed were labels, not source quotes.

answer.lead: The eight interviews do not support any of H1 to H3 as worded. H1 cannot be tested because no quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation, and the reactions to the AI are split. H2 and H3 each have statements that run against them from two participants, but those are hypothetical and in part hedged, so under a strict reading both are untested. These are patterns within this sample only, and only six of the eight participants are quoted.
paragraphs: H1 (more satisfying than traditional voice automation): P1, P2 and P3 speak well of the AI, and P4 comes round to it after an initial wish to speak to someone. P10, P5 and P1 in a second remark are unfavourable, citing the voice, the accent, the length of the introduction and an imagined car accident. The favourable remarks are comparisons with chat bots, a robot voice and repeating yourself, so the material shows approval against a poor earlier experience and does not show the comparison H1 states. Confidence: high that H1 is untested and that the reactions are split.

H2 (no immediate hang-up on learning it is an AI): P10 would have hung up at the introduction because it was too long, and P5 would probably have hung up only after being refused a human. Neither links the hang-up to learning that it is an AI. On a loose reading two participants run against H2. On a strict reading no quote tests it, and no quote says anyone would stay on the line. Confidence: medium.

H3 (no immediate request for a human): P5 says they would have asked for a human, with no timing given. P4 says the introduction is where they would probably do it, hedges that twice, and says the wish passes as the process goes on. For a decision, the usable reading is that some participants want a route to a human early in the call, while the material cannot say how many of the eight would act this way. Confidence: medium.

Why the participants react as they do is less certain than what they say. The reasons they name are the voice, the accent, the introduction, the setting and earlier experience, and P5 also names the AI itself. The link from the car accident remark to the motor claim scenario is inferred. Confidence: medium. All statements about hanging up or asking for a human come from prerecorded scenarios, P8 and P9 have no quote, and the choice of quotes is not explained. Confidence: high. A human review sample and a second coder were not part of this work, and at this decision-informing stakes that does not lower the labels.
